Dwellingplace
dwĕl´ĭng-plās
n. (a settled habitation; what the apostles did not have — Hebrew moshab, Greek astateo)
A compound of dwelling and place. The Greek behind 1 Corinthians 4:11 is a single verb, astateo, meaning to be unsettled, to have no fixed standing place.

Biblical Definition

Dwellingplace is a settled habitation, and Scripture uses it to mark three conditions. Balaam looks at the Kenites and admires their security: “Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock” (Num 24:21) — and the oracle goes on to say that the Kenite shall be wasted nonetheless. Jeremiah announces the end of an empire: “Babylon shall become heaps, a dwellingplace for dragons, an astonishment, and an hissing, without an inhabitant” (Jer 51:37) — the strongest city on earth reduced to a lair for wild creatures. And Paul describes the apostolic ministry: “Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace” (1Co 4:11). The men through whom the New Testament came had no address. Set beside the Corinthians whom Paul is ironically congratulating — full, rich, reigning as kings — the contrast is the whole argument of the chapter. Hebrews states the settled doctrine: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). A nest in a rock is wasted; a city of empires becomes a den; the apostles had nothing; and the church looks for a city whose builder and maker is God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a dwelling place as the place of residence; an abode; a habitation; the place where one lives.

DWELLING-PLACE, n. The place of residence; abode; habitation.

DWELL'ING, n. Habitation; place of residence; abode.

HABITA'TION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; settled dwelling.

CONTIN'UING, ppr. Remaining fixed or permanent; abiding; as, here have we no continuing city.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 4:11 — "Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;"

Numbers 24:21 — "And he looked on the Kenites, and took up his parable, and said, Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock."

Jeremiah 51:37 — "And Babylon shall become heaps, a dwellingplace for dragons, an astonishment, and an hissing, without an inhabitant."

Hebrews 13:14 — "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come."

Modern Corruption

Comfort and security are treated as the natural marks of God's favour on a ministry, and the apostles' actual conditions are read as an unfortunate early stage the church has since outgrown.

expand to see more

First Corinthians 4 is written against exactly this instinct, and its irony is savage: now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us — and then the apostles' own inventory, hunger, thirst, nakedness, buffeting, no certain dwellingplace. Paul is not commending poverty for its own sake; he is exposing a church that had adopted the world's measures of success and consequently despised the men who had brought them the gospel. Any ministry judged by its comfort will end by judging the apostles deficient, which is precisely the position Paul mocks.

Hebrews 13:14 gives the doctrine that keeps this from becoming mere asceticism. Here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come. The Christian is not homeless; he is between homes, and the one he seeks is permanent. That is why Balaam's Kenite nest in the rock — genuinely strong, genuinely admired — is still wasted, and why Babylon's vast permanence becomes a dwellingplace for dragons. Every earthly security is provisional, and the man who knows it is free to use one gratefully and lose it without despair.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek astateo (G790), to be unsettled, without a fixed home — 1 Corinthians 4:11 only; Hebrew moshab (H4186), a seat or dwelling; maon (H4583), a habitation or lair.

expand to see more

Greek astateo (G790) — to be homeless, without fixed standing; 1 Corinthians 4:11, its only occurrence.

Hebrew moshab (H4186) — a seat, dwelling; Numbers 24:21, Exodus 12:20.

Hebrew maon (H4583) — a habitation, den or lair; Jeremiah 51:37, and Psalm 90:1 of the LORD as our dwelling place.

Greek menousan polin — a continuing city; Hebrews 13:14, the thing believers do not have here.

Psalm 90:1 supplies the answer to the whole entry: LORD, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.

Usage

"“Have no certain dwellingplace” — said by the men who wrote the New Testament."

"“Strong is thy dwellingplace… thy nest in a rock” — and it was wasted."

"“Here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come”."
